witnesses.provenance: Solana's per-transaction MAX_COMPUTE_UNIT_LIMIT is 1,400,000 compute units. It is the chain's limit, not ours. The campaign sets ProgramTest's ceiling to exactly that value and never raises it, so a transaction that did not fit would fail rather than be re-run with headroom. The direction matters: this is a chain limit the campaign must live under, not a measurement of ours restated as a target.

Solana's MAX_INSTRUCTION_STACK_DEPTH is 5, counting the top-level instruction as depth 1, so the deepest admissible `invoke [n]` line any program can produce is [5]. A complete Dealer transition runs Dealer -> Registry, Dealer -> Claims and Dealer -> Custody, and the Claims and Custody children invoke further; this witness is what would catch a composition change that put the family one hop from the runtime's hard stop.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.error != null) | select([.logs[] | select(contains("custom program error: 0x"))] | length == 0)] | length | tostring
witnesses.provenance: The Solana runtime reports a privilege, frame, or account refusal it decides ITSELF as a bare InstructionError with no `custom program error:` log line; that line appears only when a program returned ProgramError::Custom. TIERS.md draws exactly this distinction and records a pre-taxonomy refusal as an unnamed one, because crediting it would overstate what the program proved. Every transaction in this tier is a refusal, so this witness is the whole tier's admissibility: it asserts that not one of them was bounced by the runtime before the Dealer ELF ran.

A route is EXECUTED in this census only on a succeeding transaction. This tier deliberately builds no activated release set, no admitting Core Market phase, and no Claims/Custody prestate, so nothing in it may succeed. Pinning that to zero rather than leaving it unsaid means a future change that made one of these hostile cases pass would fail the tier instead of quietly flipping a census row on the strength of a weakened refusal, which is the failure mode AGENTS.md names: do not weaken a refusal to make an integration test pass.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.label | test("into the real Registry")) | select([.logs[] | select(test("invoke \\[2\\]"))] | length == 0)] | length | tostring
witnesses.provenance: A DealerSbfError::Release refusal is only evidence about release authentication if a Registry CPI actually happened; Dealer maps a failed `invoke` and a missing/foreign return value to the same code, so the code alone cannot distinguish 'the Registry refused' from 'Dealer refused before calling it'. The chain's own `invoke [2]` line is the discriminator, and this witness requires it on every transaction whose label claims that depth. Cross-checked against the census's independent corroboration of the same logs.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.label | test("Liquidity at the")) | .error] | sort | join("|")
witnesses.provenance: Two protocol rules with no common solution. `Request::validate_shape` (crates/dclutch-dealer-codec/src/lib.rs) refuses AddLiquidity and RemoveLiquidity unless `now == 0`; `authenticate_clock` (programs/dclutch-dealer-sbf/src/lib.rs) refuses unless `now == clock.slot` for every action except Retire. A submitted transaction never executes in the genesis slot, so the shape-canonical form refuses on the Clock (code 4) and the clock-canonical form refuses at decode (code 0). This witness pins BOTH halves, which is what makes the unreachability a chain observation rather than an argument about two files. It is expected to fail the day the contradiction is fixed, and that is the point: it is the marker for a defect, not a specification of one.
